description: Apogeo Team is a multidisciplinary team passionate about space exploration and accessible technology. For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we are building an intuitive web tool that lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates. It visualizes Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon to assess power generation and direct-to-Earth communication windows. Our goal is to turn complex ephemeris and topography data.
summary: Apogeo Navigator is a free web app, in English and Spanish, that shows where the Sun and the Earth are relative to the horizon at a lunar landing site, hour by hour, and turns that into what a mission planner needs: hours of sunlight, hours of direct line of sight to Earth, time until the next sunset or Earthset, the longest night and the longest communications blackout, and a traffic-light rating for energy and communications. We queried NASA/JPL Horizons for ten real locations (Apollo 11, 15 and 17, Shackleton crater, IM-1 Odysseus, Blue Ghost 1, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e 4 and Chang'e 6) over six months (December 2026 to May 2027, hourly), so that sites and dates can be compared in minutes instead of through several expert tools: the Compare screen puts the Top 5 sites or dates side by side. Any other point of the Moon can be queried live from Horizons. The results show why the choice matters: at Shackleton crater the Sun never rises above 1.7° and Earth is above the horizon only 39% of December, while at Chang'e 4 and 6 on the far side Earth is never visible, which is why a relay satellite such as Queqiao is needed. All figures assume an ideal smooth-Moon horizon (no terrain), which the app states next to each result. The data pipeline is open and checkable: CSV uploads go through strict validation, every change is written to a hash-chained audit log, and datasets are signed with the post-quantum signature ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204) so anyone can verify them.
details:
What exactly does it do?

The user picks a lunar site and a month and sees what that site's horizon looks like. The app has these screens:

  • Home: an immersive, three-act story that starts at Shackleton crater and explains why the Moon's poles are so different from the equator.
  • Sites: a polar map with the ten sites placed by latitude around the south pole, a category filter and a card per site. A Custom coordinates tool queries any point of the Moon live from JPL Horizons.
  • Sky: a 360° panorama with the Sun and the Earth drawn at their real azimuth and elevation (the vertical scale can be magnified near the horizon, because at the poles both bodies live within a few degrees of it), a zenith view, and the time until the next sunset and Earthset.
  • Landing window: a bar of every hour of the period showing when the Sun and the Earth are above the horizon, with hours and percentages, maximum and mean Sun elevation, and the traffic light.
  • Lunar day: a timeline that plays the 29.5-day lunar day with sunrise, sunset and Earthset marks.
  • Analysis: an analysis screen.
  • Compare Top 5: a ranking of the best five sites, and a side-by-side comparison of two or three sites in the same month, or of the same site in two or three months, with a common time cursor, a metrics table with the best value marked and a one-sentence verdict. The selection is kept in the page address so a comparison can be shared.
  • Upload data: analysts drop CSV files in a pop-up, see each file validated with its status icon and save them in one step. Every file is checked against a written standard (ranges, signs, UTC format, lengths, cross-field coherence, 22 error codes) before anything is saved.
  • Sign-in, Profile and Key manager: accounts, and an administrator screen that issues post-quantum key pairs (see "How does it work?").

Two more features are worth stating:

  • Astronaut indicators. Next to the traffic light, each site shows the figures that size the hardware: the longest night (battery), the longest communications blackout (relay or data storage), the longest window with Sun and Earth up together, the mean Sun elevation during sunlit hours and the next sunsets. Each one comes with a plain sentence and the ideal-horizon warning. Examples from our data: at Shackleton the Sun sets on 2027-02-15 and does not return before the end of the data, at least 2,522 hours (about 105 days) in a row; at Chang'e 4 and 6 Earth is out of sight for at least 4,368 hours; at IM-1 Odysseus the longest full night reaches 388 hours (about 16 days).
  • Mission patches. The Apollo 11, 15 and 17 sites show their authentic mission patches, unmodified and credited "Image: NASA" (see section 7 for sources and conditions). The other sites use a neutral monogram.

Traffic light. Energy is the share of time with the Sun up (green ≥ 45%, yellow 25% to < 45%, red < 25%) and communications is the share of time with Earth up (green ≥ 70%, yellow 40% to < 70%, red < 40%); the overall rating is the worse of the two. A "sensitive to terrain" warning appears when the Sun never exceeds 3° (a nearby hill could hide it). The thresholds are provisional and set by the team.

Projection to July 2028 (administrators only). Beyond the six months of Horizons data, the app can extend the Sun and Earth positions hour by hour to 31 July 2028 with a statistical model (harmonic least squares fitted on our own ephemerides, with the synodic period refined by FFT). This view is available only to administrator accounts, so judges using the public app will not see it. We describe it here because it is part of the project and its error is measured: it is a statistical projection, not an ephemeris. We compared it with JPL Horizons over 12 months at the ten sites (and over the 13th and 14th months at only three sites). The Sun elevation error is 0.88° or less up to month 5 (October 2027), about 1.1° to 1.9° from month 6 to 11, and the model is not suitable for exact sunrise or sunset times beyond month 5. Earth elevation error stays below 1° in every month. The traffic-light colour matched Horizons in 124 of 126 site-month pairs; both misses are IM-1 Odysseus, where the share of Sun sits within 3 points of the 45% threshold. Months 13 and 14 are low-confidence. Method and full error table: docs/datos/proyeccion-2028.md in the project documentation.

How does it work?

  1. Data. For each site, the Sun and Earth apparent azimuth and elevation are requested from the JPL Horizons API as seen by an observer on the Moon (CENTER='coord@301', geodetic coordinates, no refraction, 1-hour step, 2026-12-01 to 2027-06-01, 4,369 rows per site). From those series we derive monthly metrics (hours of sun, % of sun, maximum and mean solar elevation, hours of Earth visibility) and the astronaut indicators. Each row cites its source URL. The Custom coordinates tool calls Horizons live through our backend, with rate limits to protect JPL's service.
  2. Backend. A FastAPI service on Google Cloud Run reads the CSV files from Cloud Storage and serves sites, ephemerides, metrics, sunset and Earthset times and the live Horizons query. Application data such as user accounts lives in PostgreSQL 16 on Cloud SQL, with schema changes under Alembic migrations. Uploads are validated, saved atomically with a copy of the previous version, and recorded in an audit log where every event is chained to the previous one with SHA3-256 and signed. Secrets are kept in Google Secret Manager.
  3. Integrity. A manifest with the SHA3-256 of every data file is signed with ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204). A stand-alone script, with no dependency on our code, lets anyone verify the signature and the files against a published fingerprint. The administrator key manager issues ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-65 key pairs per user under a "revoke and reissue" policy: the private key is shown once and the server never stores it.
  4. Frontend. A React single-page app (design concept "Rasante": the horizon line is the interface) hosted on Firebase Hosting. Firebase forwards /api/** to Cloud Run, so the browser talks to a single origin. The interface is available in Spanish and English.

What benefits does it have?

  • Compares sites and dates on one screen, with plain-language numbers, instead of reading separate expert tools.
  • Makes the two constraints that dominate south-polar planning, energy and a direct link to Earth, visible and comparable, and turns them into sizing figures (longest night, longest blackout).
  • Open code, open data and verifiable integrity: every number can be traced to a NASA query, and tampering with the data is detectable.
  • Accessible: the colour pairs meet WCAG AA contrast, each chart has a table alternative, the traffic light uses an icon and a word as well as colour, and the app respects reduced-motion settings.
  • Useful for education: it explains why the Moon's poles and far side are so different from the equator.

What do we hope to achieve?

A planning and teaching prototype that shortens the first screening of candidate landing sites when a mission slips and alternatives are needed. Next steps: real terrain horizons from LRO/LOLA elevation data, a full year of ephemerides, validation against QuickMap and the PGDA polar illumination products, more candidate sites once Artemis III coordinates are published, usability tests with mission planners and teachers, and, if its error can be reduced, opening the projection to all users.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python 3.12, TypeScript, SQL, CSS.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn, SQLAlchemy 2, Alembic, psycopg 3, PostgreSQL 16, cryptography (ML-DSA-65 and ML-KEM-1024), google-cloud-storage, pytest.
  • Frontend: React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, TanStack Query, React Router 7, d3-scale and d3-shape, Motion, Vitest.
  • Infrastructure (in production): Docker; Google Cloud Run (API), Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL 16, Cloud Storage (data files), Secret Manager, Artifact Registry and Cloud Build; Firebase Hosting for the front end, with a rewrite of /api/** to Cloud Run; GitHub for code and pull-request review.
  • Data service: NASA/JPL Horizons API.
  • Hardware: standard laptops; no special hardware.

Limitations we state openly

  • Ideal horizon. Horizons does not model terrain. For example, Shackleton's centre shows 100% Sun in December, but the real crater floor is in permanent shadow: the figure belongs to a smooth sphere, not to the terrain. The real terrain can only hide the Sun or the Earth, never add them, so reality is equal or worse than the figure. The relief drawn in the sky view is illustrative and does not enter any number.
  • No raster or terrain data. We did not use LRO raster products, LOLA topography, Moon Trek, QuickMap or the PGDA products as data. From the LRO we only use published landing coordinates.
  • Locations. Only Shackleton is in the south polar region, and it is the centre of the crater, a reference point and not a chosen landing site. The other nine sites are equatorial, mid-latitude, southern but not polar (IM-1 at −80.13° and Chandrayaan-3 at −69.37°) or on the far side. Blue Ghost 1 is the centre of the landing region (about ±0.01°). Artemis III candidate regions are not included because NASA has not published their coordinates; any other point can be queried live in Custom coordinates (35 days per query, not included in Compare).
  • Range. Six months of real ephemerides, not a full year. Compare works in whole months.
  • Projection. It is a statistical model with measured error, not an ephemeris; it is available only to administrators; from month 6 it is not suitable for exact times; at Shackleton, where the Sun barely rises, the colour matched by chance in some months.
  • Communications means direct line of sight to Earth with an ideal horizon. We do not model antennas, relay satellites or link budgets, and we do not compute real power or energy.
  • Viability thresholds are provisional engineering judgement, not mission requirements.
  • No user testing. We have not run usability tests with mission planners, teachers or the public; the design relies on accessibility and technical checks, not on usage data.
